issues.legal_issue: A will is proved when the propounder establishes prima facie the testator’s capacity and execution in the required manner, and the evidence as a whole satisfies the civil standard of proof without a finding based merely on unsupported suspicion.
material_facts: The claimant relied on a registered will executed by the original owner in favour of her niece, followed by a registered sale from the niece to the claimant.
Two attesting witnesses testified, and the niece’s son testified because the niece was indisposed.
The evidence described the niece’s long-term care of the testator and a natural familial reason for the bequest.
The opposing party was a stranger to the family and alleged no specific facts challenging the testator’s disposing capacity; no other relative came forward to contest the will.

The courts below relied on the testator’s age, her death shortly after execution, the registrar’s visit to her home, the niece’s absence from the witness box, the attesting witnesses’ acquaintance with the niece’s son, and the absence of medical evidence.
An earlier judgment between the same parties had considered the same will and upheld its execution, but the courts below overlooked that judgment.
issues.conclusion: The will was proved. The courts below allowed conjecture and unsupported suspicion to displace relevant evidence, so their findings were vitiated. The claimant was declared owner and entitled to recover possession.
issues.legal_principle: Proof of a will requires proof as for any other document, together with compliance with Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 and Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. The propounder must establish the testator’s competence and execution in the prescribed manner. Prima facie proof shifts the onus to a contestant who adduces material against it; the propounder must then satisfy the court affirmatively that the testator understood the will and executed it with a sound disposing mind. Suspicion warrants closer scrutiny only when it is well founded; suspicion or conjecture alone cannot replace or demolish legal proof. The court referred to R v. Hodge (1838), 2 Lewis CC 227, in cautioning against reasoning that fills evidentiary gaps by supposition.

predicates.civil_case_disputes_will: The proceeding is a civil case in which a party’s claim depends on a disputed will.
predicates.propounder_presents_prima_facie_executio: The person relying on the will presents evidence of its execution, including evidence addressing the applicable formal requirements.
predicates.testamentary_capacity_is_supported_by_ev: Evidence supports that the testator had the capacity to make the will when it was executed.
predicates.suspicious_circumstances_lack_evidentiar: Circumstances treated as suspicious are not supported by evidence establishing a genuine basis to doubt the will.

issues.definition: When a civil case disputes a will, prima facie execution evidence and evidence supporting testamentary capacity establish execution if the asserted suspicions lack an evidentiary foundation.

issues.legal_issue: A prior judgment concerning the same will may be relevant evidence in a later dispute between the same parties even when the earlier proceeding concerned different property and does not determine the later dispute by res judicata.
material_facts: The same parties had previously litigated a different property, relying on and disputing the same will.
The earlier court found that the will was duly executed, and that finding was upheld in a later proceeding between the parties.
The earlier judgment was before the courts in the present title suit, but its relevance was overlooked.
The pleadings and issues from the earlier suit were not tendered or shown to have been tried on res judicata in the present suit.
issues.conclusion: The earlier judgment was relevant evidence with a material bearing on the will’s execution, although the Court did not hold that it was conclusive by res judicata.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 11, 13 and 35 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 make the earlier judgment relevant evidence in the circumstances described. The Court also referred to Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams v. K.M. Krishnaiah, (1998) 3 SCC 331. Res judicata is a mixed question of fact and law; the Court declined to determine it because it had not been pleaded or tried below and could not be raised for the first time at the hearing before the Court.

predicates.later_civil_dispute_concerns_same_will: The later civil proceeding requires determination of a dispute concerning a will that was also in issue in an earlier proceeding.
predicates.earlier_judgment_records_adjudication_of: A judgment from the earlier proceeding records an adjudication concerning that will between the same parties.
predicates.earlier_judgment_is_before_court: The earlier judgment is placed before the court deciding the later proceeding.

issues.definition: When a later civil dispute concerns the same will, an earlier judgment recording an adjudication of that will between the same parties is relevant evidence if it is before the court.

issues.legal_issue: A plea of res judicata cannot be raised for the first time at the hearing before the Supreme Court when it was not pleaded or tried in the courts below.
material_facts: The claimant did not plead res judicata in the suit.
The pleadings and issues from the earlier suit were not tendered in evidence, and no res judicata issue was framed and tried.
The plea was not raised before the courts below or the High Court and was advanced before the Supreme Court only at the hearing.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to permit the res judicata plea to be raised for the first time before it and did not decide whether the earlier judgment was conclusive between the parties.
issues.legal_principle: Res judicata is a mixed question of fact and law. In this case, the absence of a plea and of an issue tried below meant that the plea could not be raised for the first time at the hearing before the Supreme Court.

rule.if: appeal_heard_by_supreme_court and res_judicata_not_pleaded_below and res_judicata_not_tried_below and plea_first_raised_at_supreme_court_hearing

predicates.appeal_heard_by_supreme_court: The proceeding is an appeal heard by the Supreme Court.
predicates.res_judicata_not_pleaded_below: The party did not plead res judicata in the proceedings before the lower courts.
predicates.res_judicata_not_tried_below: The lower courts did not frame and try an issue of res judicata.
predicates.plea_first_raised_at_supreme_court_heari: The party first advances the res judicata plea at the hearing before the Supreme Court.

issues.definition: In an appeal before the Supreme Court, a party cannot raise res judicata for the first time at the hearing when the plea was neither pleaded nor tried below.
